title: ABLE: Using Adversarial Pairs to Construct Local Models for Explaining Model Predictions

problem.claim: Machine learning models used in critical applications are often difficult to understand because they lack transparency.

gap.claim: Existing local explanation approaches can be unstable and have poor local fidelity.

contributions.claim: ABLE constructs local explanation models by generating adversarial pairs that bracket the local decision boundary.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly propose a novel approach called Adversarially Bracketed Local Explanation (ABLE).

author_reported_evidence.claim: On six UCI benchmark datasets and three deep neural network architectures, the authors report higher stability and fidelity than the state of the art.

narrative_sequence.summary: Opaque machine learning models create a need for interpretable explanations.
Local explanation methods approximate model behavior near a test instance with simple interpretable models.
These methods may be unstable and locally inaccurate.
ABLE generates noisy neighborhood points, creates adversarial pairs with contrasting labels, and trains a linear model on them to approximate the local decision boundary.
Experiments across six UCI datasets and three deep neural network architectures report improved stability and fidelity over the state of the art.

source_observation.claim: The method uses adversarial pairs to bracket the local decision boundary before fitting a linear explanation model.

interpretation.claim: Constructing training examples around a local boundary may improve the stability and fidelity of a simple local surrogate.

application.claim: For local explanation tasks, generate bounded neighborhood samples and boundary-bracketing counterexamples before fitting an interpretable surrogate.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify how performance varies with perturbation bounds, attack settings, datasets, or model architectures.

unknowns: The six UCI datasets and three neural network architectures are not identified.
Perturbation bounds, attack procedures, optimization details, and evaluation metrics are not reported.
The state-of-the-art baselines and quantitative results are not reported.
